 Amarius Mims — somehow the No. 18 pick in the 2024 NFL Draft — proved himself right 
 Cincinnati Bengals (NFL) By Charlie Goldsmith Published : Nov. 12, 2026 at 1:54 PM EST Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google Amarius Mims knows the names off the top of his head. Four tackles were drafted ahead of him in the 2024 NFL Draft. “Of course, it was Joe Alt, JC Latham, Olu, Tali from Oregon State and me. I was the fifth tackle.” 
 Two years later, Alt (Chargers), Latham (Titans), Olu Fashanu (Jets) and Taliese Fuaga (Saints) are all decent players on bad teams with broken offensive lines. Mims is the best right tackle in the entire NFL, and he’s on a Cincinnati Bengals’ team with the best passing game in the league. 
 In retrospect, how did Mims fall to the 18th pick in the draft?
 “That’s a good question,” Mims said. “You have to ask all of the other 17 teams that passed on me, honestly. That’s a them question. I’m thankful that the Bengals took the time to evaluate my film and actually see that just because of a lack of film and a possibility of me being ‘injury prone,’ it didn’t matter to them.”
 The word “unique” gets tossed around a lot, but Mims truly was a unique prospect in 2024. Looking back at it, Zac Taylor uses the words “Wild Card” to describe Mims’ draft profile. 
 The big number was the fact that Mims made eight total starts in college at the University of Georgia. He only was a starter for one season, and Mims missed some time that year with an ankle injury that required surgery.
 On the other hand, he was one of the most striking athletes in the entire sport at 6-foot-7 and 340 pounds with a 5.07 second 40-yard dash, 11 ¼ inch hands and an 86 ¾ inch wingspan. Mims didn’t have much college tape, but he played well when he made the first two starts of his college career in the 2022 College Football Playoff. He was even better in the six games that he played in 2023, and Mims didn’t allow a single sack in those six games during that season. 
 “You could see the talent and hope that it’d translate into something really special,” Zac Taylor said. “Our scouts had absolute conviction that he was the right pick and he could be at the level he’s playing at now. An All-Pro type of player. Those words were spoken (before the draft). Those words are rarely spoken.”
 It all worked out in the end. The 2026 Bengals get to throw the ball at what feels like an unprecedented rate because of the standout pass protection in front of Joe Burrow. Mims is the star of the offensive line. He doesn’t need help in the form of chips and double teams. He has a remarkable level of consistency in one-on-one matchups against the top defensive ends in the league. This week, the Bengals’ pass protection plan for the Pittsburgh Steelers starts with the fact that Mims can win his matchup against TJ Watt. 
 Mims is having a breakout season, making the type of star turn that’s allowing a right tackle to be a household name. At the end of the year, he’ll be eligible for a contract extension and has a case to reset the offensive line market. 
 Pretty good for a player who 17 teams passed on just two years ago. 
 “I wouldn’t change anything,” Mims said. ‘It’s a part of my journey. It’s a part of what makes me the man I am today. It’s a part of what makes me strong and what makes me a good football player. I always think about the guys that went ahead of me. Every tackle drafted ahead of me. Every player drafted ahead of me, too.”
 ***
 More than his slide in the 2024 NFL Draft, Mims is hung up on the fact that he spent the entire regular season of his sophomore year of college as the backup swing tackle at Georgia. He shouldn’t have had to wait 28 college games before he made his first start. 
 “I never shy away from saying that,” Mims said. “I don’t know what it was. I should have been starting way before I did. I know it in my heart. I should have started way before my junior year.”
 Coming out of high school, Mims was a five-star recruit and the No. 3 offensive tackle in the 2021 recruiting class. He was the top commit that year that went to Georgia. As a true freshman in 2021, he sat behind veterans Warren MccLendon (a future fifth-round pick) and Jamaree Salyer (a future sixth-round pick).
 After playing a reserve role as a true freshman, he entered the transfer portal in April of 2022. Had the transfer rules been then what they are now, Mims’ story could have taken a different turn. 
 “The only other team I’d have gone to other than Georgia would have been an SEC school, but we couldn’t transfer in-conference then,” Mims said. “Florida State was my option. I didn’t want to go to Florida State, honestly. The program wasn’t up to my standard of where I saw myself. I stayed at Georgia for obvious reasons, because of the NFL talent they’ve put out.”
 Since he stayed at Georgia, Mims got the chance to practice against six pass rushers who went on to be first-round picks. Bengals’ scouts noticed Mims in those practices, recognizing his potential in visits to Athens.
 “We had the benefit of people who had been in the school and seen him practice,” Dan Pitcher said. “We heard his coaches talk about him. We had watched him compete against high-level players on his own team. Our scouts had really high conviction. Here is this tremendously gifted guy physically who has not played very much football.”
 Georgia opened the 2022 season with McLendon at right tackle and Broderick Jones as their starting left tackle. 
 “I could have left and went anywhere else and played more (in 2022),” Mims said. “I came back (as a sophomore) just to sit on the sideline again and be a swing tackle. I should have gotten a proper chance to start, being honest with you.”
 Jones went on to be the Pittsburgh Steelers’ first-round pick in 2023. He has been a bust in the NFL. The Steelers traded him this summer, and now Jones is a backup on the Dallas Cowboys. 
 Mims says that sophomore season was the most adversity he has faced in football as well as the most frustrated that he has been.
 “It taught me that if things don’t go your way, it’s how you react,” Mims said. 
 ***
 Mims was pressed into action in the 2022 College Football Playoffs and started both games at right tackle as Georgia won the title. He took that momentum into 2023, entering the season as the starter. In the third game of the year, Mims suffered a freak injury and hurt his ankle. 
 “I had one ankle surgery because I slammed on my ankle,” Mims said. “Then all of a sudden, everyone is panicking and saying I’m injury prone.”
 Because of the ankle injury, he only made six starts in 2023. 
 “For a coach, the sample size is really small and nerve wracking,” Taylor said. “Our scouts had absolute conviction that he was going to be the player that he is. 100% conviction. Of course, was I 100% comfortable taking a guy that hadn’t started a 12 game season? I can’t say that I was.”
 The pre-draft process was especially significant for Mims, who had to prove his health, change the “narrative” about him being “injury prone” and convince teams that his inexperience wouldn’t be an issue. 
 “As a coach, you look at it as he’d have to overcome A, B and C,” Pitcher said. “You gradually work yourself to (thinking), this guy is rare. When you get a chance to bring him in, you talk to him and get a sense to feel the person, his good nature, his competitiveness. That’s how you build the entire profile as the player and the person.”
 The Bengals have a very strong history of making draft picks out of Georgia — AJ Green, Geno Atkins, Clint Boling, Shawn Williams, later Dylan Fairchild — and had behind the scenes intel. Mims visited the Bengals before the draft, and he says that he hit it off with the coaches.
 The talk leading up to the 2024 NFL Draft was that the class of first-round offensive tackles was the best in years. This was the year to pick an offensive tackle. Mims was ranked in the middle of that pack. 
 “I knew if I played my best ball, the rankings wouldn’t matter,” Mims said. “If you turn on the film, I think I’m the guy. I’m just being honest with you. I think I’m the guy. Regardless of who was drafted ahead of me, it doesn’t matter.
 The Bengals also viewed Mims as “the guy.”
 “It was beauty in the eye of the beholder,” Pitcher said. “We operate a certain way that’s going to attract us to certain types of guys. Guys like Amarius. When you’re building a team, it’s about having a vision for who you want to be and knowing what’s going to allow you to win games, and trying to find the people who fit that.”
 A massive, athletic and physical pass protector like Mims was exactly the Bengals’ type. 
 On draft day, Alt was drafted fifth. Latham went seventh. Fashanu was pick No. 11, and Fuaga went 14th. 
 The top two offensive tackles when the Bengals were on the clock at pick No. 18 were Mims at Troy Fautanu. 
 The Bengals drafted Mims. The Steelers went on to draft Fautanu with pick No. 20. Fautanu has had a nice season as Pittsburgh’s left tackle, but he’s nowhere near the All-Pro conversation that Mims has entered. 
 Drafting Mims when they did wound up being one of the franchise’s most important moves of the last few years, right up there with the Dexter Lawrence trade. 
 “I was the 18th pick,” Mims said. “Imagine if I’d have put together a whole two or three seasons (in college) like the other guys did. Imagine what would have happened if I’d have had the amount of starts that everyone else in my draft class had. But I’d never change it. I’m glad it happened the way it happened. I don’t regret falling to pick 18. I’m just thankful for the Bengals. They believed in me.”
 ***
 Before Mims, the right tackle position was a constant revolving door for in Cincinnati. The position belonged to someone different every year: Bobby Hart (2020), Riley Reiff (2021), La’el Collins (2022), Jonah Williams (2023). The Bengals signed Trent Brown to be their starting right tackle in 2024, but then he suffered a season-ending injury two games into that season. It was almost like the Bengals’ right tackle position was cursed. 
 Mims, a rookie in 2024 who spent the first two games of the year on the bench, took over as the Bengals’ starting right tackle in Week 3 of that season. It was the beginning of an era. 
 Mims showed promise but was still relatively inconsistent in 2024 and 2025.
 This year, Pitcher said, Mims is a “different animal.” 
 “As long as you have somebody who’s made of the right things from a character standpoint and a work ethic standpoint and has unique physical traits, invest in the process,” Pitcher said. “Don’t get caught in the early ups and downs. If you believe in the guy and he truly has a chance to be special, then see it through. That’s a lesson I’d take from Mims as I go forward.”
 This season, before the Bengals faced the Steelers in Week 3, Taylor met with Mims. 
 The message was, “TJ (Watt) is a heck of a player. We’re not going to fall asleep on that.”
 “I told Mims before the game and during the game, ‘Don’t have an ego about it,’” Taylor said.If you need help — a chip, a double team — the right thing to do is to ask for it.
 Mims got the message. But he didn’t need the help. Mims shut down Watt in that game (no pressures, no sacks), just like Mims has shut down everyone this season.
 “Amarius is playing at a high level,” Taylor said after that game. “He has a lot of confidence. I’m proud of the progress he continues to make, and he’s earning that.”
 Mims literally changes the math of the Bengals’ offense. Since he doesn’t need help, the Bengals can put more tight ends and running backs out in routes instead of keeping them back in pass protection. When safeties and linebackers step up to guard those tight ends and running backs, that leaves less attention on Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins.
 Burrow is being pressured at the sixth-lowest rate in the league, and his sack rate is half of what it was in 2021 (while also being the lowest of his career). 
 Mims has been the star of an offensive line that’s been playing at a very high level.
 “I’m going out there stress free, just playing ball,” Mims said. “I’m still learning. There are things I’ve got to fix. That torch hasn’t been passed to me yet. I’m doing everything I can to be the best teammate and player possible. If I’m that guy in years to come, I’ll be that guy. I’ve got some vets in my room. I don’t want to take any shine away from them.”
 He’s at a stage of his career now where he has faced all of the top edge rushers. Performances against defensive ends like Watt, Will Anderson, Myles Garrett, Aidan Hutchinson and Maxx Crosby give Mims reasons to feel very confident entering tough matchups. 
 “The amount of time I’ve put into my game, how I’ve progressed and how I’ll continue to progress, I believe in myself and the staff here believes in me,” Mims said. “They’ll put me in situations where I can show that I can be the best tackle. I’m ready.”
 Mims — not the edge rusher he’s facing — has become the headliner in those matchups this season. While he declined to share specifics, he says that at the end of seven of the Bengals’ eight games this season, the defensive end that Mims went up against has come up to Mims to compliment his game. 
 The league has taken notice of the 24-year-old right tackle who’s exactly the player that the Bengals hoped he could become. 
 “I understand that I can be that guy,” says Mims, who knew that all along.
